subject: Archaeology
title: Archaeology in War Zones
description: A quick, practical guide to Archaeology in War Zones.

hook.text: ISIS blew up the Temple of Baal Shamin in Palmyra with explosives in 2015. The explosion was filmed and broadcast.

buildup.text: War has always destroyed heritage. The Baghdad Museum was looted during the 2003 invasion — 15,000 objects vanished.

discovery.text: The 1954 Hague Convention says warring parties must protect cultural sites.

twist.text: Destroying heritage is now a recognized war crime. An ICC court convicted a militant for destroying Timbuktu's shrines.

climax.text: Satellite monitoring and 3D scanning now create digital backups of threatened sites before conflict destroys them.

punchline.text: They can blow up a temple. They cannot blow up its 3D scan.

quiz.question: What legal precedent was set regarding destruction of cultural heritage?
options: The UN declared all archaeological sites sovereign territory
An ICC court convicted a militant for destroying Timbuktu's shrines as a war crime
NATO established a permanent force to guard archaeological sites

details.summary: Armed conflict destroys archaeological sites through bombing, looting, military occupation, and neglect. Archaeologists working in war zones face physical danger while racing to document endangered heritage.
details.whyItMatters: War destroys both people and their heritage. Archaeological sites in conflict zones represent thousands of years of history that can be obliterated in moments. Protecting heritage during conflict preserves community identity and post-war recovery.
takeaways: Conflict destroys sites through bombing, looting, and neglect
Syria, Iraq, and Yemen have suffered catastrophic heritage losses
Archaeologists risk their lives to document endangered sites

faq.question: What international laws protect archaeological sites during war?
faq.answer: The 1954 Hague Convention for the Protection of Cultural Property in the Event of Armed Conflict prohibits targeting cultural sites. Its Second Protocol (1999) strengthens penalties. The Rome Statute of the ICC classifies intentional heritage destruction as a war crime.

faq.question: How do archaeologists document sites in active conflict zones?
faq.answer: Many rely on satellite imagery to monitor damage remotely. Local heritage professionals document what they can at great personal risk. Syrian archaeologists created clandestine documentation networks during the civil war.
